title: The Deadliest Snake Isn't the Most Venomous. #1 Is Tiny
description: The most venomous snake on Earth has no confirmed kills. A new 2026 study says snakes may kill up to 513,000 people a year, so who's really doing it? Here are 5 snakes, from scary on paper to the real #1. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.
sources: Ediriweera, Kasturiratne, Pathmeswaran et al. (2026) Estimates of global burden of snakebite: a literature review and geostatistical modelling study, PLoS Medicine 23(8): e1005201 — https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005201 via News-Medical (1 Sep 2026) https://www.news-medical.net/news/20260901/The-global-toll-of-snakebite-may-be-much-bigger-than-we-thought.aspx (≥2.1M–7M envenomings, 274,000–513,000 deaths, 17 years since last estimate, over half of countries lack data)

Britannica — Saw-scaled viper — https://www.britannica.com/animal/saw-scaled-viper (0.3–0.9 m, eight species, Africa to India and Sri Lanka, S-shaped folds, rubbing scales, twilight, more deaths than all other species combined in range)

scenes.say: This snake carries enough venom to kill over a hundred people. And it has never killed anyone on record.
Wait, what? The most venomous snake on Earth, and not one confirmed death? So who's actually doing the killing?
scenes.label: 0 confirmed deaths

scenes.say: Okay, so here's the thing. A brand new study says snakes may kill up to 513,000 people every single year.
scenes.label: Up to 513,000 a year

scenes.say: That's way more than scientists thought. And most of those deaths come from snakes you've probably never heard of. The real killer? You'll meet it at the very end.
So today, we're counting down five snakes, from scary on paper to the one that's actually the deadliest on the planet.
And number one? It's smaller than your arm. You can hear it before you see it. Stay for that one.
scenes.label: Stay for #1

scenes.say: Quick question before we start. Which snake do you think is number one? Lock in your guess, and let's see if you're right.
Number five is the one we just met. The inland taipan, from the dry middle of Australia.
scenes.label: Inland taipan

scenes.say: On paper, it's the champion. Guinness says one bite can carry over 100 milligrams of venom.
And the estimated human lethal dose? About one milligram. Think about that. One bite, possibly a hundred doses.
scenes.label: ~1 mg can kill

scenes.say: Its venom even carries an enzyme that helps the toxins spread through the body faster. Nature basically built a speed boost.
One male gave 110 milligrams in a single milking. Guinness says that's enough to kill 250,000 mice. Or about 125 people.
scenes.label: 250,000 mice

scenes.say: So why no confirmed deaths? Because it lives on cracked clay floodplains, out where almost nobody walks.
And here's the proof that location matters. Its cousin, the coastal taipan, is less toxic. But it has many deaths on record, especially in Papua New Guinea.
scenes.label: Weaker, but deadlier

scenes.say: And reptile keepers call it shy, even gentle. It mostly comes up in the early morning to bask and hunt.
Most known bites happened to people handling captive snakes. They got to a hospital fast, and they survived.
So lesson one: the most venomous snake isn't automatically the deadliest. Where a snake lives matters just as much.
scenes.label: Venom isn't everything

scenes.say: Number four is the snake everyone's afraid of. The black mamba, from southern and eastern Africa.
scenes.label: Black mamba

scenes.say: Okay, so it's not actually black. It's olive to grey. The name comes from the inside of its mouth, which is inky black.
It can grow up to 14 feet long, though about 8 feet is more normal. And in short bursts, Live Science says it can hit about 12 miles per hour.
scenes.label: Up to 14 feet

scenes.say: When it feels trapped, it lifts the front of its body three to four feet off the ground. Almost eye level with a child.
Then it spreads its neck, opens that black mouth, and hisses. That's a warning. It would much rather leave.
If it can't escape, it may strike again and again, then race away as fast as it can.
But if it does bite? Without antivenom, Live Science says a black mamba bite is fatal every single time.
scenes.label: Untreated: fatal

scenes.say: Some deaths have come in as little as 20 minutes, most within a few hours. So why isn't it number one? Because antivenom works, and mambas avoid people.
So far, the scariest snakes on paper aren't the top killers. But here's the twist. The next three hunt where people sleep.
And hey, if you like this kind of thing, subscribe. One wild animal secret, every day.
Number three is the common krait, also called the blue krait. It lives across South Asia.
scenes.label: Common krait

scenes.say: Here's what makes it creepy. It comes out at night. And it bites people while they're asleep.
scenes.label: Bites while you sleep

scenes.say: Doctors in Sri Lanka followed 42 krait bite patients. Every single one was bitten at night, sleeping on the floor.
Most bites happened between ten at night and four in the morning. Many families there sleep on the floor, near the ground.
scenes.label: 10 PM to 4 AM

scenes.say: And here's the scary part. Its venom attacks the nerves that control breathing. In that study, 60 percent needed a breathing machine.
scenes.label: 60% on ventilators

scenes.say: Some people didn't need a ventilator until many hours after the bite. Up to 50 hours in one case. So it can look fine, and then it isn't.
Oh, and a weird detail. Six of those 42 patients had proven bites but got no venom at all. Doctors call those dry bites.
scenes.label: Dry bites

scenes.say: The krait is one of India's Big Four, with the cobra, Russell's viper and the saw-scaled viper. Guinness says together they cause up to a million bites a year.
scenes.label: The Big Four

scenes.say: Still, the krait isn't the worst. Number two kills tens of thousands of people every year in just one country.
Number two is Russell's viper. Chunky, about three to five feet long, covered in a chain of dark spots.
scenes.label: Russell's viper

scenes.say: When it's threatened, it lets out a long hiss. One of the loudest of any snake in Asia.
It loves farm fields and grain stores, because that's where the rats are. And where the rats go, people work.
Now here's the big number. A huge 2020 study estimated India alone loses about 58,000 people to snakebite every year.
scenes.label: 58,000 a year

scenes.say: That's about 1.2 million deaths in twenty years. And Russell's viper is one of the main snakes behind them.
scenes.label: 1.2 million

scenes.say: Here's how hidden it was. Government hospitals counted 15,500 snakebite deaths in thirteen years. The study found about 154,000 in the same period.
scenes.label: 10x undercounted

scenes.say: The study says the lifetime risk of dying from a snakebite there is about one in 250. In some areas, one in 100. And over a quarter of victims were kids under 15.
Most bites happen in the rainy season, at dusk or at night, to farmers and their kids walking home.
Its venom stops your blood from clotting. And the kidneys can fail a day or three later. So fast treatment really matters.
Doctors usually start with ten vials of antivenom. But many small hospitals don't have nearly that many.
scenes.label: 10 vials to start

scenes.say: And still, it's not number one. Because number one is in India too, and in Africa, and in the Middle East.
Number one is the saw-scaled viper. And yeah, this tiny thing is it.
scenes.label: Saw-scaled viper

scenes.say: It's only about one to three feet long. Smaller than your arm. Easy to step right past in the dark.
scenes.label: 1 to 3 feet

scenes.say: Remember, I said you can hear it first? When it's scared, it coils into S-shaped loops and rubs its rough side scales together.
That makes a hissing, sizzling sound. Like frying oil. It's a warning. And it's quick to strike.
scenes.label: Sizzle warning

scenes.say: There are eight species, from Africa through Arabia to India and Sri Lanka. It hunts at twilight, right when people walk home.
Britannica says that in their range, these vipers are believed to cause more human deaths than all other snakes combined.
scenes.label: More than all others

scenes.say: Think about that. Not the biggest. Not the fastest. Not the most venomous. Just small, common, and right where people live.
And that brings us back to that new study. Scientists modelled snakebite across the world for the first time in seventeen years.
They found at least 2.1 million people get envenomed every year. Maybe as many as 7 million.
scenes.label: 2.1 to 7 million

scenes.say: Deaths: at least 274,000 a year, and up to 513,000. And Africa south of the Sahara carries almost half.
scenes.label: 274,000 to 513,000

scenes.say: In Africa, farmers often walk unlit paths at night without boots, and the nearest antivenom can be hours away.
On top of the deaths, more than 800,000 survivors are left with lasting disabilities every year.
scenes.label: 800,000 disabled

scenes.say: Here's the final twist. In over half the countries with venomous snakes, nobody even writes most bites down. So no one saw the real number.
The good news? Bites are treatable. Better maps, more antivenom, and faster rides to hospital could save huge numbers of lives. The WHO wants to cut snakebite deaths in half by 2030.
So, the deadliest snake isn't the one with the strongest venom. It's the one that lives closest to us.
Okay, be honest. Was your guess the saw-scaled viper? Tell me in the comments which snake you picked.
scenes.label: Your guess?

short.title: Most Venomous Snake, Zero Confirmed Kills
short.header: Why the inland taipan isn't the deadliest
short.description: The inland taipan has the strongest venom of any land snake, but no confirmed human deaths. Here's why. Full countdown of the 5 deadliest snakes on my channel.

scenes.say: The most venomous snake on Earth has never killed anyone on record.
It's the inland taipan. Guinness says one bite can carry over 100 milligrams of venom, and about one milligram may kill a person.
One male gave enough venom in a single milking to kill 250,000 mice. Or about 125 people. So why no confirmed deaths?
Because it lives on empty cracked clay in the middle of Australia, where almost nobody walks. And it's shy.
Meanwhile, a tiny saw-scaled viper, smaller than your arm, is believed to kill more people than almost any snake alive.
Snakes kill up to 513,000 people a year. But not this one. The most venomous snake on Earth has never killed anyone on record.
